newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - Hungary sacks state privatisation board.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Hungary sacks state privatisation board.

text.p: The Hungarian government sacked the entire board of the state privatisation agency APV Rt on Friday, saying it had made irregular payments amounting to millions of dollars to a lawyer.
But the government spared Tamas Suchman, the minister in charge of APV, although opposition parties said he was responsible and should go.

"The government decided to remove the chairman of the board, the deputy chairman and all members of the board from their posts with immediate effect," government spokesman Elemer Kiss told reporters at a news conference.
The order dismissed, effective immediately, 11 members of the board of directors, Kiss said. The seven members of the supervisory board would be sacked following approval by parliament.
Kiss said the board had authorised irregular payments to Marta Tocsik, who was acting as a lawyer on the APV board's behalf in negotiating asset transfers to local municipalities.

Tocsik had two contracts with APV, one of which was awarded without competitive bidding. They gave her eight to 10 percent of the amounts she saved for APV and Kiss said the money Tocsik received amounted to 804 million forints ($5.2 million).
"The investigation found several breaches of the law, irregularities and diversions from APV's internal rules," Kiss said.
He said the government would ask Tocsik to return the money and if she did not agree would initiate legal proceedings.
The government has also initiated criminal proceedings against persons involved in the deal with Tocsik, he said.
Asked if Suchman had known about agreements with Tocsik, Kiss said he did know about one of the contracts but had asked that it be corrected.
He said the government overall was pleased with the conduct of the privatisation of Hungary's state-owned enterprises, one of the main programmes of the post-communist administrations.
"APV has made at least 1,300 decisions as part of a successful privatisation process," Kiss said. "This was the only scandal in the operations of APV."
But opposition leaders continued to demand the resignation of Suchman, one of the leading figures in Prime Minister Gyula Horn's Socialist Party.
"We believe Suchman is responsible for this and we continue to demand his resignation," said Andor Nagy, cabinet chief of opposition party Fidesz.
Tamas Deutsch, another high-ranking Fidesz official, said Suchman had sent letters to several municiplaities saying that Tocsik was APV's appointed representative.
"It's inconceivable that the government didn't know of a case involving hundreds of billions of forints," Deutsch said, referring to the value of the shares to be transferred to the municipalities.
"Ultimately the prime minister is responsible for what his government does," Deutsch told Reuters.

Suchman, who was also recently appointed Minister of Industry and Trade, has said he did know of one contract and while not wanting to anticipate the outcome of the inquiry, he considered it unethical.
Kiss said a new board of directors for APV was likely to be set up within a few days.
